$comment: Shared deployment-output conformance table.
`ruvyxa build` writes a `deploy` section into `manifest.json`: the
provider-agnostic description of what the build produced and how it must be
served. Eleven adapters, the standalone server, and the Rust host all have to
agree on two questions that this section answers once:
1. Which routes may a CDN answer from a file, and which must reach the
function. Getting this wrong is silent: publishing an ISR page as a
static file means the host serves the build-time snapshot forever and
the function that owns revalidation is never invoked, so ISR and PPR
quietly become SSG. Three adapters had already grown their own
`excludeStrategies` list before this table existed.
2. What cache-control each class of emitted file carries. The same two
policies were hand-written in the Rust static handler, the standalone
server, and four adapters; one of them had drifted.
Replayed by crates/ruvyxa_cli/src/deploy_manifest.rs (Rust, the writer) and
by tests/packages/ruvyxa/deploy-manifest.test.mjs against
packages/@ruvyxa/core/src/deploy-manifest.ts (JavaScript, what every adapter
reads). A rule added to one side and not the other fails there rather than
in somebody's production deploy.
Cache-control by class of emitted file. `client` chunks are named by the
hash of their contents, so a URL never changes meaning and the answer is
immutable. `asset` covers everything published from `public/`, whose URL
is chosen by the author and can change meaning on the next deploy.
`document` is a pre-rendered page: safe to cache, never safe to pin,
because a redeploy replaces it under the same URL.
Paths the framework owns. A host that serves the publish directory before
invoking the function must still forward these, and no route may claim
one. Kept level with FRAMEWORK_ENDPOINTS in the endpoint conformance
fixture.
How each route is served, given its kind, strategy, and whether the build
produced a document for it. `static` means a file the CDN may answer
directly; `function` means the request must reach the server.
`why` is the reason, not decoration: every one of these was a decision
somebody has to be able to re-derive.

cases.why: A fully baked page with no revalidation clock. The whole point is that no server is involved.
A dynamic SSG route with no matching static params was never rendered, so there is no file to serve.
The shell is a fixed document; everything else happens in the browser.
The function owns revalidation. Serving the baked file directly pins the page to its build-time snapshot forever.
The pre-rendered part is a shell; the dynamic holes are filled per request.
An API route is code, not a document.

$comment: What a function returns with a document it rendered, by strategy. ISR
advertises its own clock so a CDN in front of the function can hold the
page for exactly as long as the project asked.
The stale window is `expire - revalidate` with `expire` fixed at one year,
which is the formula Next.js ships in production. It has to carry a number:
RFC 5861 defines `stale-while-revalidate=<delta-seconds>` and Netlify's CDN
documents only the numeric form, so a bare directive is dropped there and
the page stops being served stale while it refreshes.

cases.why: `0` means revalidate on every request and is a value, not an absence. `revalidate || 60` reads it as missing and pins the page for a minute, which is the difference between a live page and a stale one.
An ISR route that never named a window falls back to the shared default, and both lanes have to pick the same number.

A revalidate at or past the one-year expire leaves no stale window. Subtracting has to saturate at zero: an unsigned wrap would emit a stale window of eighteen quintillion seconds, and a signed one a negative directive every CDN drops.
